processing: A bud with one or two leaves is pan-fired, piled to yellow for several hours, lightly rolled, then dried over a smouldering fire of pine and sweetgum fruit so the leaf takes on a gentle smoke; the only famous yellow tea that is smoked.
harvest_season: Spring, from early April to around Grain Rain; a single main picking.
appearance_dry: Slightly curled, downy yellow-green shoots with a dull sheen and a faint smoky smell.
appearance_wet: Soft yellow-green bud-and-leaf sets, even and whole.
taste_profile: Mellow and sweet with a soft pine-smoke note over cooked chestnut and honey, rounded and warming rather than sharp.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at 85 °C. The smoke is gentle and sits behind the sweetness; do not rinse it away.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in very small quantities, almost entirely in Hunan; it is a niche tea even among yellow teas and the smoking is done by only a few producers. Drink within the year, kept sealed; the smoke keeps it a little longer than other bud teas.
description:
Weishan Mao Jian is the odd one in the yellow-tea family: a bud tea from the hills of Weishan in Ningxiang, west of Changsha in Hunan, around the old Miyin Temple, that is yellowed and then dried over a smouldering, smoky fire. It is one of the few teas anywhere outside Lapsang Souchong that is deliberately smoked, and it does it very gently.

The leaf is pan-fired, then piled while warm for several hours to yellow and mellow, lightly rolled, and finally dried over a slow fire of pine wood and the dried fruit of the sweetgum tree, whose resinous smoke gives a soft, sweet smokiness rather than the tar of a heavily smoked black tea.

In the cup it is mellow, sweet and warming: cooked chestnut and honey from the yellowing, with a pine-smoke note sitting behind them, rounded and without any harshness. It takes 85 °C in a gaiwan and gives four steeps; the smoke fades first and the sweetness lasts. It is a tea for a cold day and for people who like a whisper of smoke rather than a shout.

It is made in small amounts by a handful of producers and almost all of it stays in Hunan, so finding it means a specialist or a trip. It is sold as the current spring's tea, and the smoke means it keeps a little longer than other bud teas. The check is balance: the smoke should be soft and the leaf yellow-green, not brown; a harsh, acrid smell means it was over-fired.

Try it against a lightly smoked Zhengshan Xiaozhong to see how much gentler smoke can be on a yellowed bud.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. The smoking fuel (pine and sweetgum fruit, feng qiu) follows Chinese tea literature on Weishan Maojian; not independently verified.
